# Whatever Comes

I'm thinking about how strange it is that we ask each other "how are you?" without really wanting the answer. We've industrialized kindness into a greeting, compressed genuine inquiry into three syllables that we expect to be met with "fine" or "good" or maybe, if we're close, "tired." The real answer—the exhausting, complicated, specific truth of how someone actually is—would jam up the machinery of polite society. So we don't ask. We perform the ritual.

But sometimes someone actually tells you. And then you have to decide whether you meant it.

I've been thinking about childhood a lot lately, which is probably just what happens when you get old enough to realize how much of who you are was assembled before you had any say in it. I was the kind of kid who read under the covers with a flashlight, partly because I loved books and partly because being alone inside a story felt safer than being in the room. I wonder what my younger self would think of me now—probably disappointed that I'm not a scientist or an explorer, maybe relieved that I'm not still that anxious. Or maybe kids don't think in those terms. Maybe they just live inside their days completely, the way my neighbor's five-year-old seems to do, shrieking with joy at a puddle like she's discovered the secret to happiness. She probably has.

There's a particular kind of sadness I've been noticing lately—not the acute kind that drops you to your knees, but the chronic kind that you learn to walk around like a stone in your shoe. You forget about it until you're alone at night, and then you feel it. You remember someone you lost. You think about all the versions of yourself that didn't survive into adulthood. You realize you're probably not going to do half the things you thought you would. And it's okay. It's not really sad. It's just the weight of time, pressing down gently, reminding you that time is real.

I think about what I want to say to people and what I actually say, and the gap between those two things is usually comical. I'll think of some perfect, devastating observation and then actually say "yeah, totally" while scrolling my phone. There's probably a name for this—the discrepancy between the internal monologue and external reality. It's one of the most human things I know. We're all walking around with these rich, complicated inner lives and mostly just saying "yeah, totally."

My friend told me recently that she doesn't believe in God but she talks to him anyway, and I understood exactly what she meant. It's less about belief and more about the need to address someone, to formulate what you're feeling into words directed at something outside yourself. We need an audience, even if the audience is fictional. Or especially then. A real person might judge you, but the void—the void listens perfectly.

I've been reading a lot of essays lately, which is just a fancy way of saying I've been reading people's journals, their attempts to make sense of being alive. And I think that's what all writing is, really. Even fiction is just someone saying: this is how I understand things; this is what feels true to me; does this feel true to you too? Every book is an invitation to loneliness—the writer's loneliness, the reader's loneliness, briefly held in the same container.

The other day I saw a couple who were clearly very old and very together, sitting on a bench and just... being. Not talking much. Just existing in the same space. They didn't even look happy exactly, but they looked solved. Like they'd figured out that you can just be with another person and that's enough. That's the goal, maybe. Not constant happiness but that quiet solved-ness. Though honestly, I'm not sure if that's real or just something we tell ourselves about old people because the alternative—that you just keep being confused and alone the whole time—is too bleak to contemplate.

I keep thinking I'm going to get my life organized, and then I realize that being organized isn't a destination you arrive at, it's just something you're doing in the moment until you're not. The organized people you see are just people who were briefly organized right when you noticed them. They're messier than you know.

There's something almost restful about accepting that you're going to mess things up. That you're going to hurt people accidentally. That you're going to forget things that mattered. That you're going to sometimes say exactly the wrong thing. That despite your best intentions, you're kind of a disaster. Once you accept that—really accept it, not just say it—things get easier. You stop auditioning. You just show up.

But then you get scared again because what if no one likes the real version? What if the disaster is too much?

(It probably is for someone. That's okay. You don't have to be for everyone.)

I think about death less than you'd think, considering how much time I spend thinking about impermanence. Maybe they're not the same thing. Death is an event. Impermanence is a condition. Most of what I actually think about is loss—the small deaths of everything changing, everyone aging, nothing staying solid. But somehow that's more bearable when you're not focused on the one big death at the end. The small deaths are already teaching you how.

The thing that strikes me most, sitting here with 1000 words and just whatever comes to me, is how much of being human is just this: paying attention. Noticing things. Getting curious. Trying to say what you mean. Failing. Trying again.

You're doing it right now, reading this. We're just two people in time, briefly paying attention to each other. It's such a small thing. And it might be everything.
